title: Gateless Barrier, Case 26: Fa-yen: Two Monks Roll Up the Blinds
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk highlights how our minds often get caught up in seeking happiness through external means, such as others' approval or possessions, rather than finding it within ourselves. This pattern is rooted in a lack of understanding and can lead to attachment and craving, causing us to lose sight of the present moment. By embracing the unknown and letting go of these patterns, we can cultivate a clear mind, calm heart, and sense of satisfaction that comes from within, rather than relying on external sources of happiness.

sentences.text: Before I give the talk I prepared, I wanted to open with something like a public comment period about the practice period.

The back story is that we're thinking, next year, 2020, how could it be 2020, that the theme of the various talks and teachings, as much as we can fit it in, might be to really explicate and explore the chant book.
There's a lot of stuff in there: what does this all mean, where did it come from?
The practice period starts in the middle of January and goes through the beginning of March.
I signed myself up to give a class.
We don't have a [unclear: "shoe"], so I had student this year, so I'll do the class.
And so I figured I should do something from the chant book.
I was going to do what we just chanted at the end there, the merging of difference and unity, which is a pretty interesting Zen poem, very cool and philosophical and subtle and all that stuff.

But then, at Rohatsu, we ended our ceremony about Buddhist enlightenment by dedicating it to all of our ancestors, and we did a traditional list of names, which are all men, the traditional ancestors list, and then we did a wonderful little chant about our ancestors who are women.
And that's in the chant book now.

So I was thinking the other option, this is the [unclear: "Kama period"] question, you can tell me now, tell me later, during the [unclear: "Kama period"], is maybe instead of the merging of difference and unity, we should do a class on the first Buddhist women who are listed in that chant.
I have control of the website and I can change the topic.
I don't think anybody has signed up yet.
Anybody signed up yet?
Would anybody be disappointed if we changed it?
No?
So anyway, you can think about that.
And then look forward to lots of talks, hopefully by all the senior students and practice leaders and me, about what the heck all this stuff is in the chant book.
You're all chanting it as if it meant something to you.
Maybe it does.
And do we have to understand things in that way exactly?
Case 26 of the Mu Mon Kong.
*When the monks assembled before the midday meal to listen to his lecture, the great Fai Yang of Jing Myong pointed at the bamboo blinds.
Two monks simultaneously went and rolled them up.
Fai Yang, the teacher, said, one has got it, one has lost it.*
This last line, where apparently he's talking about the two monks who jumped up to help him: one has got it, one has lost it.
Other translations say, one gain, one loss, or one gains, one loses, which seems to point even more to a person.
One gains, one loses.
So let's say that it's a story about gain and loss.
That's a good place to start, because that's what we're all about, right?
We're always trying to get something.
We're always trying to avoid losing something that we want to hold onto.
Although sometimes we really look carefully at our motivations and our actions, we also try to gain things that we really don't want and try not to lose things that we really should let go of too.
So it's not so simple.
But we're so involved in gain and loss all the time, aren't we?
What do I get out of that?
We have much more sophisticated ways of asking that question, right?
We say, what's the theme of tonight's whatever?
Can you tell me more what the intention of this whatever is?
What I really mean is, what do I get out of this?

And maybe it's true that these teachings point to this: an endless quest to be happy or satisfied, or something like that, that's based on gaining what you want and not losing what you don't want to lose, is probably doomed to failure, right?
It's never quite going to work out, whether it's about rolling up blinds or about relationships.
And preparing this, I was well aware that here I would be, flapping my lips, saying that.
It's a lot easier to say that it is indeed foolish to look for happiness in gain and loss, or look for happiness in external things, or in a way even internal things.
Where do we find happiness?
Where are we looking for that happiness?
It's easy to say we're probably looking in the wrong places, harder to shift our patterns.
Where do you look for happiness?
A teacher's approval?
A lover's devotion?
A parent's acceptance?
My parents are still living, but it seems like I'm meeting a lot of people now who are looking for the acceptance of their parents who are no longer alive.
I was like, wow, tough road to home.
Are we looking for a co-worker's admiration?
Or if we're really paying attention to even just the little things: it would make me happy if this driver would let me go first at the four-way stop.
They didn't, or they did.
Is there a way that we're constantly putting our happiness in other people's hands and expecting them to do the right thing for us?
So gain and loss, and he points at the blinds, which isn't usually a time the teacher would talk, right?

We just had our wonderful Rohatsu sesshin, and at the beginning of the meal I wouldn't usually, in this case I give a few [unclear: "aria instructions"] or something, but I wouldn't usually point at somebody and say, one gains, one loses.
So it's something here was really important for him to say.
If I even look at anybody funny, I hear about it later.
So something was important here about these two monks rolling up the blinds.
So the teacher here, Fai Yin, we've met before.

I don't think we've met him so far in the Mumonkan, but we've met him before in one of my other most favorite stories, which is another story I feel like I'm always talking about, and if I look carefully I don't know if I'm really living it so well, but little by little.
So remember the story that Fai Yin, well, I'll tell you the back story and then we'll see if you remember the story.
So the back story, this earlier story: this is when Fai Yin was a student, and he had been a long time at his teacher Dixiang's monastery, and it was time to move on.

It was common in the training then to stay quite a number of years in one monastery, and then, usually with the teacher's approval, but not always, sometimes they just slip off, you go off on a pilgrimage and visit other monasteries and have encounters with the teacher, some of which end up getting codified in these stories.
Where have you come from?
What is Buddha?
And one of the back story things that I always think about, which always makes me happy about our wilderness program, is that China's a big place, and there was no public transportation.

So these monks were walking for days or weeks or even months, doing lengthy, lengthy quiet walks across the countryside, along the roads and trails and over the mountains, to go to some monastery that they'd heard about, finally get there.
What a moment that would be, right?
You walk for a month.

For us it's a privileged thing to be a backpacker and do the PCT or something, and this was just a normal thing: walk for a month, you knock at the front door, somehow you get showing into the teacher, right?
Big deal.
And this idea of pilgrimage does actually go on today.

Way back when Norman asked me to ordain, which surprised the heck out of me, I had a strong impulse to do this practice, so I went on multiple retreats with other teachers that I'd met before, and I rounded up teachers that I knew but had never met, had formal interviews with, and I asked them.
My teacher asked me to ordain.
What does that mean?
What does that mean?
And the favorite response I remember is from Kyogen Carlson, who I've mentioned before, who died suddenly five years ago or so.
I asked him this question in Dokusan.
He looks at me a minute and says, God help you.
So this practice of pilgrimage still goes on today.
It's a great practice.
You could do this practice.
You could go to other centers.
It takes a little chutzpah.
You sign up for the interview, even though the teacher's never heard of you before, and you go in and you ask your question.
So anyway, Fai Yang is getting ready to do this, and he's at the gate of the monastery with his traveling sandals and his staff and his hat, and his teacher, Di Jiang, sees him there.
Probably knew he was going to be there, but in the story he sees him there.
So Di Jiang asked Fai Yang, What is your journey?
What is your journey?
Fai Yang says, Going around on pilgrimage.
Di Jiang said, What do you expect from pilgrimage?
Fai Yang said, I don't know.
Di Jiang approved and said, Not knowing is most intimate.
Not knowing is most intimate.
So in this case, which is connected to the later Fai Yang, this must have been a big question for Fai Yang: gain and loss.
So his teacher asked him what he expected, and he didn't start musing about what he was going to get out of this, right?
Which is what we would probably do, right?
Oh, I think I'm going to learn a lot, and it'll be interesting, it'll probably be hard.
We'd go on like this, and he was just like, I don't know.
So not knowing is most intimate, and this is really hard for us to live, right?
Our minds are so primed to have all kinds of theories and predictions about what's going to happen.
What am I going to gain?
What might I lose?
I was talking at the retreat about another great story a little later in this collection, a whole story about balancing on top of a 100-foot pole.
And the story suggests that with our great Dharma power, we can actually get to where we can sit on top of the 100-foot pole.
We're balanced there.
The pole is probably doing its thing, but we're balanced sitting.
But then that koan says, well, yeah, good job and all that stuff, but now you've got to jump off.
Now you've got to step off.
And stepping off is all about not knowing, isn't it?
We don't know what's going to happen when we step off the 100-foot pole.
So the teacher asks for a favor, or the teacher makes a request, points to the blinds.
Of course we jump up to help, but what are we gaining?
What are we losing?
When we're going through our lives, we do think we know.
At least, maybe we recognize it's a little provisional, but we have a pretty good idea.
But what are we going to gain?
What will I gain from this job or this relationship or going to the Dharma hall or whatever?
And we're always a little worried.
What am I going to lose?
What will I lose?
Will I lose my autonomy?
Will I lose my strength and my health?
What will I lose?
Will I lose myself?
And so we make these predictions, but are they actually accurate?
I'm not sure if they are.
I think we could all study this and see.
Are my predictions about gain and loss, when faced with the decision, right?

One thing I've noticed that's pretty concrete, and these are such sharp moments that I notice them: when my mind imagines, like it does catastrophizing, and imagines the disaster that's going to happen, that disaster never happens.
Sometimes a different disaster happens, but it's never the one I would have anticipated.
Have you noticed that?
Something you didn't even think of happens.
It makes you wonder why we spend all this energy imagining what's going to go wrong.
Not only are we wrong about what's going to go wrong, we're blind to what is going to go wrong, so there's no point in worrying about it.
We have no clue.
So gain and loss is also a reference.
Everything in these koans is a reference to something.
It's part of what makes them so interesting and also so frustrating and opaque.
Gain and loss is a reference to a famous early Buddhist teaching called the Eight Winds of the World, eight winds that blow around.
I've mentioned it a few times.
It's really important, I think, and interesting.
Gain and loss are two of the eight winds of the world.
The basic idea of the Eight Winds of the World is how foolish it is, and how habitual it is, to pin all our hopes on having more gain and less loss.
So gain and loss are the first two.
Second are more fame and less infamy.
You lived on in infamy.
We don't like that.
Oh, sorry, praise and blame are separate.
So even back then the Buddha was really interested in fame and praise and blame.
There's fame and infamy as one, and there's more praise and less blame as the other.
That plays out here, right?
We always want praise, we don't want blame.
And the fourth pair is the biggie: more pleasure, less pain.
We put our happiness on hoping for more pleasure and less pain.
These kinds of teachings are easily misunderstood as nihilistic or masochistic or something like this.
It's not saying that we shouldn't enjoy praise and fame and gain and pleasure when they show up.
They're pleasant: oh, that's nice.
But we are so easily and unknowingly habituating ourselves to crave these things, and to fear the other, to crave pleasure and fear pain.
So it's really powerful conditioning that Fayen is pointing to.
One gains, one loses.
Gain and loss, right here, just rolling up the blinds.
And it's probably important that it's a pretty innocuous-sounding thing.
It's like, yeah, just rolling up the blinds?
There's gain and loss?
Dang.
What about the big stuff?
What about life and death?
What about sickness and health?
What about will I ever really be loved?
Big gains and losses.
A nice little piece of writing on the Buddhist perspective on happiness popped into my inbox today, conveniently enough, from one of the magazines, Lion's Roar, I think.
There are three different teachers that they ask this question: what is happiness in the Buddhist frame?
I want to share one of the three.
This is the Venerable Thupten Chodron.
She's a good person to know about.
She's an American-born Tibetan Buddhist nun ordained by His Holiness the Dalai Lama, so in that lineage, the Galukpa school of Tibetan Buddhism.
Thupten Chodron is the abbess of an actual abbey, a little monastery in northeast Washington.
I don't know why it's there.
Maybe because the land was cheap or somebody gave it to them?
I don't know.
It's a place called Srivasti Abbey.
I've never been there.
Next sangha trip, we should drive a little further.
Kind of might have been there.
There are a lot of really beautiful thangkas.
Anyway, here's Thupten Chodron, Venerable, talking about happiness.
And you will not be surprised to know she's going to refer to the Eight Winds of the World, or the Eight Worldly Concerns.
*There are many different types of happiness.
Some are selfish, others are not.
Some forms of happiness rely on people, objects, places, sounds and so forth.
Since we cannot control our environment to the extent we'd like, happiness that depends on people and things is neither stable nor predictable.
In addition, our motivation to experience this kind of happiness is often self-serving.
We're seeking only our own happiness and our mind is trapped in what the Buddha called the Eight Worldly Concerns.
Attachment to wealth, praise, good reputation and sense pleasures.
And aversion to loss, blame, notoriety and unpleasant sensations.
The Buddha directs us that the happiness that comes through spiritual development, such as the joy that arises from single-pointed concentration, the Buddha directs us to that happiness.*
Sorry, I said that wrong.
*The Buddha directs us to the happiness that comes through our spiritual development, such as the joy that arises from single-pointed concentration.* Those moments are just like, ah, it's right here.
*We may think this is self-serving in cases in which someone becomes attached to the bliss of deep states of concentration.
It might be.

However, a practitioner cultivates concentration with the intention to then use their focused mind to realize the nature of reality, to understand the nature of reality, or to cultivate other virtuous qualities, such as great love and great compassion.
Selfishness is not involved.
Those of us who grew up in Christian contexts have a tendency to think that to be a truly compassionate spiritual person, we must sacrifice our own well-being.
The greater our suffering, the purer our compassion for others.
Now, the Buddha does not share this view.
In fact, any who have attained Buddhahood have fulfilled their own purpose and others' purpose as well.
Attaining the Dharmakaya, the omniscient, compassionate mind of a Buddha, is the fulfillment of one's own aim.
And gaining a Buddha's form bodies, with the capacity to manifest in various ways to work for the benefit of others, is the fulfillment of others' aims.
In that work, a Buddha also experiences great bliss, but this is not self-serving.*
I talk a little bit different in her tradition.
We don't talk a lot here about gaining the multiple bodies of the Buddha, but that's what we're doing too.
*For us ordinary beings, joy comes from being free from craving.
By diminishing our craving and attachment, we may not have that giddy excitement that we call happiness, but our minds are clear and our hearts are calm.
There is more self-acceptance and thus greater satisfaction in our lives.
In addition, a sense of fulfillment arises when we cultivate kindness and compassion towards others.
We delight in being of service to others and in using our unique talents in whatever way possible to contribute to others' well-being.
We're involved with others, so we are free from arrogance, jealousy, and competition.
Our mind remains peaceful, and we spread peace simply with our presence.
When we look at sincere Dharma practitioners from all Buddhist traditions, we see they are happy, contented people, and their lives are meaningful for others.
That certainly is not self-serving.*
So that's the end of what Thubten Chodron said.
I think in the Zen tradition, we would agree with all that, just fine.
But we also emphasize something else, which is this idea of not knowing.

As we practice letting go of our thinking and our knowing of how things are and who we are and who you are and how it's all supposed to go, if we open to curiosity and not knowing, that's a great catalyst that makes all this stuff she's talking about possible.

When we're so sure of where the gain is and where the loss is, so sure what's in it for me, so sure how this is and how it goes, it narrows us down and we can't really practice the way she's talking about.
We can try.
We can put on the mantle of looking like we're practicing, but we're not really practicing.
We're just trying to have more gain and less loss.
And don't forget the Heart Sutra, which we just chanted in Sino-Japanese, so maybe we didn't understand it as well, but you know that in there it says there's no gain and no loss.
It says right in there.
And no gain, no loss used to be the exact words, but the translation we're doing now talks about increase and decrease to mean the same thing.
The part that says, *all dharmas are marked by emptiness.
They neither arise nor cease, neither defiled nor pure, neither increase nor decrease.* So increase and decrease, gain, loss.
I think the other thing here is just really practical and a good idea.
If we get too worried about gain in our practice, we just get frustrated.
Have you noticed this?
We sit down like, I'm going to figure this out, or I'm going to go to this retreat and I'm going to work on my thing.
I've been practicing for how long and I still have that stupid thought?
Oh, I suck, right?
So it doesn't seem to work that way.
It's not going to work to impose the logic of gain and loss on our practice.
It so helps us to lighten up about that.
It's not that things don't change.
It's not that practice doesn't have benefit.
Things do change over time in our lives, and practice for sure is really beneficial, but not always in obvious, measurable ways.
X minutes of zazen does not lead to y degree of result ever.
Sometimes years of slogging zazen leads to nothing.
Other times, one breath.
Oh, yes.
So it's a nonlinear kind of gig, for the geeks out there.
Like we did, as I mentioned, we just had this really wonderful, powerful Rohatsu sesshin that ended on Sunday morning.
And I noticed that everybody, me included, felt really good when it ended.
We're all happy.
Aren't we all happy?
We were so happy that day.
What were we happy about?
I think if you took somebody aside and you said, "Oh, you look so happy.
What did you gain from this sesshin?" they'd be like, "I don't know.
It's really happy."
Maybe they would attribute it to, I don't have to sit there anymore.
It's relief of survival.
But I don't think that's true.
It's not just relief of survival.
There's something we all did benefit from in that practice, and we benefit from tonight, and we benefit from every day.
But we really don't know what it is.
You can't say, I gained this, or I lost that, or I didn't lose that.
So there's no gain and loss.
And everything's changing.
Every case in the Mumonkan does have a verse and a short commentary from Master Wu Men, which they call Mumon in Japanese.
I don't always share them, but I noticed Alison did.
It's more like the typical pattern to read the case and read the verse and read the commentary.
His stuff's so opaque, I usually don't want to bother you with it.
But I like the poem for this one.
So this is Master Mumon reflecting on these two monks, jumping up to roll up the blind.
*When they are rolled up, the great sky is bright and clear, but the great sky still does not match our way.
Why don't you throw away that sky completely?
Then not a breath of wind, not a breath of wind will come through.*
*When they are rolled up, the great sky is bright and clear, but the great sky does not match our way.
Why don't you throw away the sky completely?
Then not a breath of wind will come through.*
That's great, huh?
I guess I'm out of talk.
Good thing.
Mm-hmm.
Thanks.
Thanks.
They are...
